content:
The Formal Frontier Team of the Mathlib Initiative is happy to announce a Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization of the main theorem of Bloom–Sawin–Schildkraut–Zhelezov, *The sum-product conjecture is false for real numbers*.

Repository: https://github.com/mathlib-initiative/sum_product

The formalized headline theorem is:

SumProduct.sumProduct_false

The corresponding Mathlib-only challenge statement is viewable in the Lean playground.

This is a conditional formalization. The Lean theorem assumes

SumProduct.MartinetTotallyRealTowers

which is the paper’s Martinet-tower input: asymptotically good totally real class-field towers with bounded root discriminant. This result depends on class field theory and the Golod–Shafarevich criterion, and is not currently available in Mathlib. The hypothesis should also be part of the Lean FRO evaluation suite soon; see leanprover/lean-eval#385. Thus the formalization proves, in Lean, that Martinet’s theorem implies the failure of the real sum-product conjecture.

Under that explicit hypothesis, the theorem proves that there is an absolute c > 0 such that there are arbitrarily large finite sets A ⊆ ℝ with

max |A + A| |A * A| ≤ |A|^(2 - c).

The repository also includes comparator wrapper files, and the headline theorem has been checked with leanprover/comparator against a Mathlib-only challenge statement.

We also take this opportunity to promote a proposed metadata standard for formalization projects: a root-level formalization.yaml.

Specification: https://github.com/mathlib-initiative/formalization.yaml

The idea is that formalization repositories, especially AI-assisted ones, should report in a standard, machine-readable way:

  • what was formalized;
  • what remains conditional or imported from the literature;
  • how source statements align with Lean declarations;
  • what axioms and sorries are present;
  • how the work was produced;
  • what review or audit has happened;
  • and where the formalization deliberately diverges from the source.

This is in line with our mission of establishing standards and best practices for automatic formalization. As the field advances quickly, as illustrated by this rapid formalization of a very recent result, we want reporting norms for assumptions, provenance, fidelity, and review to mature alongside the tools.

In this project, formalization.yaml records the Martinet hypothesis as an explicit literature dependency, documents the conditional scope of the result, lists the main Lean declarations, points to the comparator configuration, records production/provenance information for the AI-assisted development, and states the current review caveats.

It also records the tools used to produce the formalization: human-directed sessions with Claude Code, OpenAI Codex through codex exec and pi, and a custom asynchronous multi-agent worker/reviewer orchestrator for the Dedekind-zeta support library, with builds and axiom checks used as gates.

We are also explicit about limitations. The current review status is self-assessed and agent-audited, not independent external peer review, and the repository has not undergone a code-quality or Mathlib-style review. These caveats are part of the published metadata.

The schema is still evolving, and we will continue working with the community to refine it; see AI authored projects > bridgeland stability @ 💬 for a previous version.
Discussion thread: #Autoformalization > Discussion: the sum-product counterexample

If you are interested in joining the team working on the Formal Frontier Project please get in touch with me, especially if you have experience orchestrating long-horizon AI agents.

The Mathlib Initiative has budget to hire contractors to join us in this effort. It would be a short term contract (probably 2 -- 4 months) and well compensated.
